name: Ivan Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential; you can tell me the public line and your private view. What's a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that builds appointment software for community clinics. I fix duplicate slots and test text reminders, with a senior developer checking the hard changes. My two-year college diploma got me in, but I still ask for help on complicated database work. I use AI tools every day to explore fixes, then compare the result with a clinic's real appointment list.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household and local work situation?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs electrical systems on regular contracts, and our children are eight and fifteen. We have a mortgage, I earn well for a junior developer, and we've saved around ten months of expenses. Plenty of software employers are nearby. I like experimenting, but a patient who misses a visit is a real person, not a tidy test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the assistant can draft routine reminder tests, provided a person checks the clinic list before sending anything. It saves me a little time now. I would use that time to sit with the receptionist who gets the angry calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and my partner's repair contracts would hold up. Ten months saved means a late client payment would not threaten the mortgage. I still want our product to do what clinics actually need, with or without fancier AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing duplicate appointments with senior review and use the assistant only on test records before checking the clinic list. We'd continue putting new pay into savings each month. In the first year I'd spend one paid hour a week with the clinic receptionist if the company agrees, learning which reminder errors hurt people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The work is stable and our bills are covered. A little less typing could let me learn the part of the job I keep missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you ask the receptionist about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month two reminders went to the same patient for different times. I'd ask the receptionist what happened when the patient arrived. The code passed its test, and the visit still went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company won't give you that hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the test list and ask again at the next review. I wouldn't leave the paid job to do volunteer research at a clinic. We have a mortgage even with savings.

I'd spend any **time saved** learning from receptionist calls if paid time is available.
think: I expect both **household wages** to continue and the mortgage to stay covered.

do: Keep **fixing duplicate slots** with senior review and checking clinic lists.
Continue **monthly savings** from new pay and learn from receptionists during paid time if approved.
feel: **Calm** about current pay and work, with interest in improving patient reminders.

steps.text: Keep checking duplicate appointment fixes against real clinic lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AI can write reminders and routine code, so we should test errors with clinic staff and ask how many junior roles remain. I'd bring the receptionists into the trial, not just developers. I'd also attend the staff committee meeting about paid learning time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could run a good trial and still lose junior hours when the company needs fewer people. My daily AI use doesn't make me the one person management must keep. My partner's contracts and ten months saved help us breathe, but our mortgage still needs wages over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd learn the firm's new AI scheduling tool by testing a duplicate-slot case with a receptionist during paid hours. I'd attend the staff committee meeting and ask for a written junior-hours plan. If my hours fall in the first year, we'd stop the planned home repainting and I'd apply to nearby clinic-software support posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I want to try the tool and hear the receptionist's verdict. I don't want the trial used as a quiet reason to erase the junior rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which duplicate case would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the patient who got two times for one visit, with names removed. If the tool says both appointments are fine, the receptionist can show exactly where the patient waited. I'd record that mistake before a wider launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell colleagues your own hours are at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after management gives us numbers. I'd say I am a junior and much of my work is routine. A strong demo isn't a promise about the next pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could do our scheduling code and clinic replies before robots reach hands-on electrical repair around 2031. I'd ask for a written layoff timetable and a person clinics can call about a missed visit. I would not promise our junior team survives because patients still come through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my coding wage could disappear. Ten months saved and my partner's repair contracts give us time, but two children and a mortgage make a long search expensive. Nearby software firms may face the same cheap AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd ask for a manager reference and put an extra amount from each pay cheque into savings while both wages hold. I'd speak to the clinic operations lead about paid appointment-coordinator openings and ask the staff committee for a clear notice period. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I'd apply for a paid coordinator role only if there is a vacancy and its wage with my partner's covers mortgage and school costs; I'd enroll in a clinic-records course only if a public grant or employer pays the fee and the schedule fits school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can ask around and learn quickly, but I expect a large part of our income to go. Ten months of savings are a bridge, not a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the clinic operations lead first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether coordinators are still being hired and what they are paid. A friendly conversation isn't a job offer. I want the hours in writing before I change our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the committee seek beyond notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid training before layoffs and a way for clinic staff to challenge bad automated reminders. We should have the receptionists at that meeting. A patient should not lose a visit because the software closed a complaint.

say: I'd demand **written layoff dates** and clinic appeal routes as thinking AI reaches code in 2028.
I'd explain that **2031 repair robots** come after the threat to our screen work.
think: I expect my **coding wage** could end despite a strong cushion.
Our **ten-month savings** and repair contracts buy time, but cannot carry the mortgage indefinitely.
do: Save **extra new pay** while both wages hold and request a manager reference tomorrow.
Ask the **staff committee** for notice and paid training before cuts.
Apply for **paid clinic coordination** after layoff only if wages cover family bills; enroll in funded training if pickup fits.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of a major household wage despite ten months saved.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings are a bridge, not a new wage.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 thinking AI** from later robots affecting electrical repair.
The committee request connects **notice and paid training** to clinic staff's appeal rights.
A coordinator move requires **real wages and vacancies**; study needs funding and school-pickup fit.

Enroll in clinic records course only with public or employer funding and school-pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for yearly junior staffing numbers and ask clinic staff to name the reminder mistakes that cost a patient a visit. Thinking AI reaches our code by 2031, while robots may affect my partner's electrical repair around 2034. Five years is enough to run a small test now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at finding where an appointment goes wrong, but I don't know if a clinic will pay me for that after AGI. A small experiment feels possible while both wages arrive. I won't spend our ten-month reserve to prove an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd spend no more than 90 from new discretionary pay, after mortgage and school costs, to learn a new AI workflow for simulating twenty appointment clashes using invented records. I'd ask a receptionist to review the results during paid work time if my manager approves; if not, I'd use only invented cases and stop at the 90 cap. We'd add a fixed amount from my developer pay toward twelve months saved while both wages hold. In the first year after 2031, if coding hours shrink, I'd apply for paid clinic software-testing posts only where vacancies exist and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs, before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy in a useful way. The test may show I'm better at this work, or show that AI can do it without me. Either result is cheaper to learn while I still have a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the 90 pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short supervised lesson in building simulated appointment cases and the small software fee for the test. I would use no patient names. If the fee rises, I stop; the ten-month buffer is for our family, not a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a good test make you leave the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A clinic saying the test helped isn't a paid opening. I would keep the developer wage until a written offer covers the mortgage and school costs with my partner's income. A useful test is evidence, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell newer developers to ask clinic staff where a scheduling mistake actually hurts a patient. A decade before 2036 gives us time to test small ideas and learn work beyond code. Thinking AI reaches our screens before robots may reach my partner's repair work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By my early fifties I might have a stronger record of fixing appointment problems, though AGI could make that cheap too. We have ten months saved, regular repair contracts and local software options today, so the next few years feel secure. I'd use time to collect evidence, not promise the children a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer wage and regular savings transfer, and add one invented scheduling case to my test library each month. If a clinic employer funds both fee and paid time for a records course, I'd take it; otherwise I'd spend at most 150 from new discretionary pay on a required course only when paid vacancies ask for it and ten months of essentials remain untouched. In the first year after 2036, if coding hours shrink, I'd apply for paid clinic testing or operations roles before giving notice, and leave only for a written offer that with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later demand, calm about the bills in front of us. I can make one small case each month without asking the family to bet its reserve. The actual vacancies will tell me whether the extra learning is worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the test library?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use invented reminders for a patient who changes times twice, then note what the receptionist would need to correct. No real patient record goes in it. A small case can show a mistake without making anyone's health details my portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs more than 150?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the employer will pay both the fee and learning time. If not, I'd wait rather than cross the cap or touch ten months of essentials. I won't buy a course just because its title sounds safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect junior coding to shrink before I have a paid clinic skill, and ten months saved won't replace a career. Written notice, funded records training, paid clinic openings and a human way to correct missed visits would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets blamed when a patient misses a visit after two conflicting reminders. Our clinic dashboard says both appointment reminders went out; the receptionist sees the empty chair. I want that person in the room when we decide the tool works.

headlineQuote: Our clinic dashboard says both appointment reminders went out; the receptionist sees the empty chair.
portrait: Ivan is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, fixing community-clinic appointment software while learning.
He earns **higher junior pay**, shares a mortgage and two school-age children with an electrical-repair partner, and has ten months saved.
He uses AI **daily**, testing its suggestions against clinic lists and receptionist experience.
The **2028 shock** alarms him because cheaper thinking work could end his wage before a paid clinic move.
Longer timelines let him test **invented appointment cases** within a small cap while protecting the ten-month reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior coding wage before paid clinic work is available.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded records training, paid openings and a human missed-visit appeal would help.
